summary: This proposed standard defines how DTLS, RTP, RTCP, STUN, TURN and ZRTP packets are multiplexed on a single receiving socket. It overrides guidance in RFC 5764 on the topic, so one port can handle all these kinds of traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: When a media application uses one network port for everything, the receiver has to work out from each arriving packet which protocol it belongs to. This RFC rewrites the rules for that decision, so that the key exchange, the encrypted audio and video, the network-traversal messages and the relay channels can all share a port without their number ranges colliding.

questions: multiplex dtls rtp stun on one port
how to multiplex stun dtls and rtp on one port
what is the first byte range for dtls
subtitle: How one UDP port can carry STUN, ZRTP, DTLS, TURN channels and RTP by looking at the first byte.

tldr.problem: RFC 5764 lets a media receiver work out what an arriving packet is by looking at its first byte, so that DTLS, STUN and SRTP can share one port. The ranges it set aside collided with ranges other registries were already using, and it left no room for ZRTP or for TURN channels.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reworks the demultiplexing algorithm: STUN takes the first-byte values 0 to 3, ZRTP takes 16 to 19, DTLS keeps 20 to 63, TURN channels take 64 to 79 and RTP keeps 128 to 191, with anything else dropped. It also rearranges the STUN method and TLS ContentType registries so that a future allocation cannot silently break multiplexing.
tldr.outcome: One port can now carry all six kinds of packet under a scheme that still has room for more, and the IANA registries carry an explicit coordination warning. RFC 7983 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5764 and was later updated by RFC 9443.

facts.label: TURN channel overhead
facts.value: 4-byte prefix, against 36 bytes of STUN overhead

today: RFC 7983 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5764, and it was itself updated by RFC 9443. It has not been obsoleted, so the demultiplexing ranges it defines are the ones to implement.

sections.title: Why the Original Scheme Had to Be Fixed
sections.content:
Section 5.1.2 of RFC 5764 defines a scheme for a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) receiver to demultiplex DTLS, STUN and SRTP/SRTCP packets that arrive on the RTP port, so that one port can carry the encrypted media and the key exchange that sets it up. The scheme works by looking at the first byte of each packet. Unfortunately, it created four problems.

First, it implicitly allocated codepoints for new STUN methods without an IANA registry reflecting those allocations. Second, it did not take into account the fact that ZRTP also needs to be demultiplexed with the other packet types explicitly mentioned in Section 5.1.2 of RFC 5764. Third, it implicitly allocated codepoints for new TLS ContentTypes without an IANA registry reflecting these allocations. Fourth, it did not take into account the fact that TURN's use of STUN can create TURN channels that also need to be demultiplexed.

Overlapping ranges between different IANA registries become an issue when a new codepoint is allocated in one of these registries without carefully analysing the impact it could have on the other registries when that codepoint is demultiplexed. Among other downsides of the bad design of the demultiplexing algorithm, it creates a requirement for coordination between codepoint assignments where none should exist, and the RFC calls that organizationally and socially undesirable. Because RFC 5764 has been widely deployed, there has to be awareness of this issue and of how it must be dealt with. So even if the feature related to a codepoint is not initially thought to be useful in the context of demultiplexing, the relevant IANA registry expert should at least raise a flag when the allocated codepoint irrevocably prevents multiplexing.

The RFC states two goals. The first is to make sure that future allocations in any of the affected protocols are done with the full knowledge of their impact on multiplexing, achieved by updating RFC 5764 and modifying the IANA registries with instructions for coordination between the protocols at risk. The second is to permit the addition of new protocols to the list of multiplexed protocols in a manner that does not break existing implementations. At the time of writing, the flaws in the demultiplexing scheme had been unavoidably inherited by other documents, such as RFC 7345 and SDP-BUNDLE, so those and any other affected documents need to be corrected with the updates this document provides.
sections.plainLanguage: The original rules took values out of the numbering systems of other protocols without saying so, so two unrelated protocols could end up with the same number and be confused on the wire. This RFC sorts out the ranges and tells the registries to watch out for each other from now on.

sections.title: STUN Method Codepoints
sections.content:
The demultiplexing scheme in RFC 5764 says the receiver can identify a STUN packet by looking at the first byte: if the value of this byte is 0 or 1, the packet is STUN. The problem with this implicit allocation is that it restricts the codepoints for STUN methods to values between 0x000 and 0x07F. That in turn reduces the number of possible STUN method codepoints assigned by IETF Review, the range 0x000 to 0x7FF, from 2048 to only 128, and eliminates the possibility of having STUN method codepoints assigned by Designated Expert, the range 0x800 to 0xFFF.

To preserve the Designated Expert range, the RFC allocates the values 2 and 3 to also identify STUN methods. The IANA registry for STUN methods is modified to mark the codepoints from 0x100 to 0xFFF as Reserved. Those codepoints can still be allocated, but they require IETF Review with a document that will properly evaluate the risk of an assignment overlapping with other registries.

The registry itself is rearranged from two ranges into three. It used to be 0x000-0x7FF by IETF Review and 0x800-0xFFF by Designated Expert. It becomes 0x000-0x07F by IETF Review, 0x080-0x0FF by Designated Expert, and 0x100-0xFFF Reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: STUN messages were quietly borrowing the first two numbers of the method numbering space, which left only a fraction of it for real methods. The RFC gives STUN four numbers of its own and reserves the rest for the multiplexing scheme.

sections.title: Adding ZRTP
sections.content:
ZRTP is a protocol for a media path Diffie-Hellman exchange to agree on a session key and parameters for establishing unicast SRTP sessions for Voice over IP applications. ZRTP is media path keying, because it is multiplexed on the same port as RTP and does not require support in the signalling protocol.

In order to prevent future documents from assigning values from the unused range to a new protocol, the RFC modifies the RFC 5764 demultiplexing algorithm to properly account for ZRTP by allocating the values from 16 to 19 for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: ZRTP is a second way to agree on the keys for encrypted media, done on the media path itself rather than in the signalling. It needed a range of its own, and this RFC gives it four numbers.

sections.title: TLS ContentTypes
sections.content:
The RFC 5764 scheme dictates that if the value of the first byte is between 20 and 63 inclusive, the packet is DTLS. For DTLS 1.0 and DTLS 1.2, that first byte corresponds to the TLS ContentType field. Considerations must be taken into account when assigning additional ContentTypes in the codepoint ranges 0 to 19 and 64 to 255, so this does not prevent demultiplexing when that functionality is desirable.

The RFC notes that RFC 5764 describes a narrow use of DTLS that works as long as the specific DTLS version used abides by the restrictions on the demultiplexing byte, the ones that this document imposes on the TLS ContentType Registry. Any extension or revision to DTLS that causes it to no longer meet these constraints should consider what values may occur in the first byte of the DTLS message and what impact it would have on the multiplexing that RFC 5764 describes.

The registry gains an explicit warning. The codepoints 0 to 19 and 64 to 255 are marked as unassigned and requiring coordination, and the middle of the old range is split out: 25 to 63 becomes plain unassigned, while what used to be 25 to 255 becomes 64 to 255 requiring coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: For encrypted media, the first byte of a packet is the type of the TLS record, and the values from 20 to 63 already belong to that meaning. The RFC marks the values on either side of that range as needing a conversation with the multiplexing rules before anyone uses them.

sections.title: TURN Channels
sections.content:
When used with Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE), an implementation of RFC 5764 can receive packets on the same socket from three different paths: directly from the source, through a NAT, and relayed by a TURN server. Even if the ICE algorithm succeeded in selecting a non-relayed path, it is still possible to receive data from the TURN server. When ICE is used with aggressive nomination, the media path can quickly change until it stabilizes, and freeing ICE candidates is optional, so the TURN server can restart forwarding STUN connectivity checks during an ICE restart.

TURN channels are an optimization where data packets are exchanged with a 4-byte prefix instead of the standard 36-byte STUN overhead. The problem is that the RFC 5764 demultiplexing scheme does not define what to do with packets received over a TURN channel, because these packets start with a first byte whose value is between 64 and 127 inclusive. If the TURN server was instructed to send data over a TURN channel, the demultiplexing scheme specified in RFC 5764 will reject these packets. Current implementations violate RFC 5764 for values 64 to 127 and instead parse packets with such values as TURN.

To prevent future documents from assigning values from the unused range to a new protocol, the RFC modifies the demultiplexing algorithm to properly account for TURN channels by allocating the values from 64 to 79 for this purpose. This modification restricts the TURN channel space to a more limited set of possible channels when the TURN client does the channel binding request in combination with the demultiplexing scheme described in RFC 5764.
sections.plainLanguage: When traffic is relayed, the relay can wrap each packet in a short label instead of the usual heavy STUN header. Those labelled packets had no home in the old rules, so the RFC gives them a range of sixteen numbers.

sections.title: The New Demultiplexing Algorithm
sections.content:
Section 7 replaces the text in Section 5.1.2 of RFC 5764. The receiver looks at the first byte of the packet. If the value of this byte is between 0 and 3 inclusive, the packet is STUN. If the value is between 16 and 19 inclusive, the packet is ZRTP. If the value is between 20 and 63 inclusive, the packet is DTLS. If the value is between 64 and 79 inclusive, the packet is a TURN Channel. If the value is between 128 and 191 inclusive, the packet is RTP, or RTCP if both RTCP and RTP are being multiplexed over the same destination port. If the value does not match any known range, the packet MUST be dropped and an alert MAY be logged.

The old text had only three ranges: 0 or 1 for STUN, 20 to 63 for DTLS, and 128 to 191 for RTP. Everything else was undefined, and the new text also says what to do with a packet that matches nothing.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is now a single lookup table on the first byte of the packet, with a clear answer for every value, including an instruction to throw away anything unrecognised.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is short here. The document updates existing IANA registries and adds a new range for TURN channels in the demultiplexing algorithm, and these modifications do not introduce any specific security considerations beyond those detailed in RFC 5764.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing which numbers mean what does not add any new risk here. The security rules of the document it updates still apply.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Three registries are touched. The STUN Methods registry gains a registration for the reserved codepoints 0x100 to 0xFFF, named as reserved for DTLS-SRTP multiplexing collision avoidance, which cannot be made available for assignment without IETF Review, and its ranges are reassigned as described earlier: 0x000-0x07F by IETF Review and 0x080-0x0FF by Designated Expert.

The TLS ContentType registry gains two reserved entries: the values 0 to 19 and the values 64 to 255, each described as unassigned and requiring coordination, with the DTLS-OK field recorded as N/A for both.

The TURN Channel Numbers registry gains a reservation of 0x5000 to 0xFFFF, named as reserved for DTLS-SRTP multiplexing collision avoidance.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps three lists of numbers that this scheme depends on, and each one now carries a note saying which parts are off limits and why.

data.title: The DTLS-SRTP receiver's packet demultiplexing algorithm
data.code:
+----------------+
|        [0..3] -+--> forward to STUN
|                |
|      [16..19] -+--> forward to ZRTP
|                |
packet -->  |      [20..63] -+--> forward to DTLS
|                |
|      [64..79] -+--> forward to TURN Channel
|                |
|    [128..191] -+--> forward to RTP/RTCP
+----------------+
